In this garden, Software Project pages model software products: applications for end users, libraries, frameworks, CLIs, desktop or web apps, editors, runtimes, and the like.

, , and model the current page shape: a linked H1 title, the repository and star count directly beneath it, then lean descriptive bullets. , , and show the naming instinct—short root-level pages—but predate this shape and lead with prose or an unlinked title; follow them for naming only, not for the first block.
How to name the main page for a software project

Give a software entity a root-level one-word or short main page when its primary name is not confusing and it is either reputable or nascent but likely to grow sub-namespaces for shortcuts, config, docs, or related notes. A short main name leaves room; long names (owner/repo or person/project) make every child path longer and harder to work with. Example: rather than Person/Jesse Duffield/GitHub/Lazygit. Aliases can point from other namespaces, such as Programming/Language/Rust or Person/Name/GitHub/Project, to that main page when useful.
How to name the main page for a software project

When the garden is tracking a company or person context, some projects may stay under that sub-namespace for situational awareness. If one of those sub-namespace pages is a software entity and later becomes heavily used in the garden, refactor it: give it a root-level page and add an alias from the old path. Example: this garden originally had Anthropic/App/Claude Code because the focus was on the company; after more content and Claude Code becoming a cultural force, it got its own page with an alias to the old location.
How to name the main page for a software project

Having more than one rule here is intentional but can feel confusing. The aim is to avoid spamming the top level with every similar piece of software, and to use placement as a subtle signal: root-level primacy for software that has "arrived" or is clearly going to grow; under company or person when we're tracking it in context of that entity.
How to name the main page for a software project
When we treat something as a software project

Strong signals: GitHub or similar repo links, official project homepages, article or post titles that name a software project, or notes that describe a tool, editor, library, app, CLI, or server. We may infer a software entity from context; when we do, we note that in the report.
When we treat something as a software project

Check in this order: exact main page name, exact alias, partial title match, repo owner and repo name, then page-body mentions of the same homepage, repo, or description. Classify as: existing, similar, new, or blocked.
Shared frontmatter conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.

To mark a page as a software project instance, add logseq-entity:: pointing at this type page (the namespace uses nested segments: Logseq/Entity/Software/Project). The type page then gets backlinks to all software project pages.
Software-project-specific frontmatter can include created-by:: pointing to a person or company page when the creator entity is clear.
File: pages/<ProjectName>.md. In links, use the main page name with forward slashes for namespaces where we use them (e.g. Lazygit/Keyshort/Some action).

The first block is an H1 whose text links to the project: - # [ProjectName](url). The H1 link points to the project's canonical home—its homepage when it has one, otherwise its repository. Descriptive prose never shares the H1 line; the description lives in child bullets below it.

The top-of-page links come first, directly under the H1 and before the description. When the project has both a homepage and a repository, the H1 links the homepage and the first child bullet links the repository. When it lives only on a repository, the H1 links the repository and no separate repository bullet is added.
Each external location appears exactly once. A repository already linked at the top is never repeated in a later "Source repository" or "Links" bullet.
After the links, keep the page lean: a few descriptive child bullets. State the implementation language on its own short bullet (for example, "Written in .") rather than folding it into prose.
When the project is hosted on GitHub, include the count when available: record the count with a dated source-check day on the repository line (or on its own bullet when the repository is the H1).

In this garden, UI Area pages model one named region of a product's interface — a panel section on hardware, or a view or bar in software — and list the controls and smaller areas inside it.
A region the product's own documentation names and that holds controls: Microfreak/UI/Oscillator, Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar, Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View.
<Item>/UI is the root area for an item and covers its whole interface, the way <Item>/UG holds its Logseq/Entity/Book/User Guide.
A single knob, button, pad or field is a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control, not an area.
A small group of controls stays a heading on its area page rather than becoming a page, even when the documentation names it, such as the Transport Controls section of Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar.
A UI Area corresponds to an ; a root <Item>/UI page or a full view such as Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View corresponds to an .
A Logseq/Entity/UI/Control corresponds to an . A preset or a saved Live Set, which fills the interface with real values, corresponds to an and is modeled by its own entity.
Place an area at <Item>/UI/<Area>, nesting a smaller area under the area that holds it: <Item>/UI/<Area>/<Sub-area>.

A hardware panel can also be mapped by position. Each side of the device is an area, <Item>/UI/Front or <Item>/UI/Rear; a side laid out in rows has one area per row at <Item>/UI/Front/Row/<NN Row>, numbered top to bottom, such as Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/02 Main.

Inside a row, or on a side without rows, each item takes a two-digit number counting left to right: 01 Matrix, 02 Paraphonic Button. A numbered group of controls is an area, such as Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/01 Matrix; a numbered single control is a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control.
Use the name printed on the panel or used in the manual, in Title Case: Oscillator, Control Bar, Arrangement View, Scrub Area.

Search <Item>/UI and the item's older pages before creating an area. When the garden already has a page for the same region under another name, link it from the area page, and list the older name in alias:: when it has no page file of its own.
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Area]]; up:: links to the containing area, and a root <Item>/UI page links up:: to the item. See Logseq/Frontmatter for shared conventions.
One bullet-wrapped H1 with the area's name, then one sentence saying where the area sits and what it is for, then a picture of the area when the user guide has one.

A ## Controls section links each Logseq/Entity/UI/Control in the area, in panel or screen order. A ## Areas section links smaller areas when there are any. Link rather than embed; control pages are short and many.
A ## Source section links the user guide or manual section that describes the area.
Microfreak/UI/Front → Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top → Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/01 Matrix
Ableton/Live/UI → Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View and Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar
A Launchpad page would follow the same shape at Launchpad/UI/<Area>, for example its grid of pads.
In this garden, UI Control pages model one thing a person operates on a product's interface — a knob, button, pad, fader, switch, field or slider — so any control can be linked by name.
A control the product labels or its documentation names: Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Timbre, Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record.
On hardware, a physical control; in software, an on-screen control, including draggable markers such as a loop brace or a locator.
A menu command with no control on screen belongs under the item's menu pages, such as , and a keyboard shortcut is a . A control page links to both when they exist.
Place a control at <Item>/UI/<Area>/<Kind>/<Name>, under the Logseq/Entity/UI/Area that holds it.
<Kind> is the noun the product's documentation uses for that control, singular and in Title Case: Knob, Button, Switch, Toggle, Field, Slider, Menu, Pad, Fader, Marker, Jack, Strip.
<Name> is the label printed on the panel or used in the manual.

On a panel mapped by position, a numbered single control carries its kind in its own name, <Row>/<NN> <Name> <Kind>, as in Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/02 Paraphonic Button. A control in a numbered group keeps <Group>/<Kind>/<Name>, and when the group has only one control of that kind the name is left off: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/01 Matrix/Knob.
A control that selects among named modes has one page per mode beneath it, and a parameter that only exists in one mode has its page beneath that mode: Logseq/Entity/UI/Control/Setting.
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Control]] and up:: to its area. See Logseq/Frontmatter for shared conventions.
One bullet-wrapped H1 with the control's name and kind, then one sentence on what it does.
A picture of the control cropped from the user guide's panel figure, kept on a Logseq/Entity/Asset/B2 page at <Control>/Asset/Panel/png.

Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:

Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:

Optional blocks, in this order, when they apply:
Ableton Live: Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record, Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Set Locator
Launchpad: a pad at Launchpad/UI/<Area>/Pad/<Name>; describes one pad set up as a toggle.
A proposal for describing how a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control changes its value, apart from the protocol that carries it. Not yet a preference.
Form — what the control is physically or on screen: knob, button, pad, fader, field. The <Kind> segment of a control's page name records the form, in the product's own word.
Behavior — what happens to the value when the control is operated. The same form can behave in different ways: a Launchpad pad can be a toggle, a momentary button or a trigger, as in .
MIDI is one way to carry a control's value to another device. A behavior describes the control itself; a MIDI CC number or a MIDI mapping goes under the control's Remote control block.
Momentary — on while held, off when released.
Trigger — fires one event when pressed and keeps no state, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Arrangement View/Button/Set Locator.
Toggle — alternates between two states on each press, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Button/Arrangement Record.
Multi-state toggle — steps through three or more states in a fixed cycle on each press.
Unipolar — a value from zero up to a maximum, such as 0–127 or 0–100%.
Bipolar — a value centered on zero that runs from a negative minimum to a positive maximum, such as Length on Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/Sample/Length, from -100 to 100.
Relative (endless) — sends increments and decrements with no fixed end; the device keeps the value.
Selector — moves through a fixed list of named positions, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type.
Numeric field — holds a number typed in or dragged, such as Ableton/Live/UI/Control Bar/Field/Arrangement Position.
Encoder with push — a rotary control whose press acts as a separate button.
Pressure — adds a continuous value to a pad or key while held, such as aftertouch.
Position on a surface — a fader, slider or touch strip whose value follows a position along a line, or an XY pad that gives two values at once.
Whether each behavior gets its own page under this one, so a control page can link to it.
Whether a control page records its behavior in a property such as ui-control-behavior:: or in a body line.
How to model a control whose behavior depends on a mode, such as a knob that is bipolar in one oscillator model and unipolar in another.
In this garden, UI Control Setting pages model one mode a Logseq/Entity/UI/Control selects, one parameter that exists only in such a mode, or one gesture that gives the control another function.
A mode: one named position of a selector, such as the oscillator model Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog.
A parameter: the name another control takes while that mode is active, such as Microfreak/UI/Oscillator/Knob/Type/VAnalog/Detune, which the Wave knob sets.

A gesture: a way of operating the control other than its plain use, such as pressing a knob, holding a button, or using the control while Shift is held: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/06 Save Button/Hold.
A plain value along a range, such as 64 on a knob, is not a setting page.
A mode sits at <Control>/<Mode>, beneath the control that selects it; a parameter sits at <Control>/<Mode>/<Parameter>.
A gesture sits at <Control>/<Gesture>, named Press, Hold or Shift. A gesture that combines two nests the second beneath the first: Microfreak/UI/Front/Row/01 Top/02 Paraphonic Button/Hold/Shift.
Use the names the display or manual shows.
Frontmatter: logseq-entity:: [[Logseq/Entity/UI/Control/Setting]] and up:: to the control or mode above it; prev:: and next:: follow the order of modes in the manual when the modes are numbered.
One bullet-wrapped H1, then one sentence on what the setting does.
A parameter page names the control that sets it, with a link.
A Source line links the user guide or manual section.
In this garden, YouTube Video pages model one identifiable video published on YouTube.
The YouTube video ID is the deduplication key. Search youtube.com/watch?v=<id> and youtu.be/<id> across pages before creating a page, regardless of title, channel, or page namespace.

A page that merely embeds or cites a video while documenting another subject is not a YouTube Video instance. A raw transcript child page is part of its parent video's notes, not a second video entity.

Prefer <creator>/YouTube/<YY>/<MM>/<short title> when the publishing creator and publication month are known. The creator may be a person, company, organization, or software project. Preserve an established video page's path when marking an existing instance.
A video in an ordered run can instead live beneath a series hub, with a published ordinal before its short title. Logseq/Entity/Series governs ordinals and ordering.
logseq-entity:: with Logseq/Entity/YouTube marks a video. Add Logseq/Entity/Series after it when the video is an installment of an ordered series.

Record date-created:: from the video's publication date when verifiable. Link its known year through logseq-created-time-year:: to a matching page. Shared property conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter.
Lead with a bullet-wrapped H1 that links to the video's watch URL. Name the publisher or speaker when known; keep any synopsis and notes beneath the heading.
A {{video ...}} block is useful when inline playback or timestamped notes are part of the page. Notes with clickable {{youtube-timestamp ...}} headings nest beneath that video block.

When a video is also a podcast episode, its page lists first in logseq-entity::. That page holds the shape for the combination: video seconds for every timestamp, chapters as headings, snips, highlights, and frames for what only the video shows.
A YouTube playlist is a separate entity modeled by Logseq/Entity/YouTube/Playlist. A video's playlist membership does not change its video identity.
In this garden, YouTube Playlist pages model one identifiable playlist published on YouTube.
The YouTube list ID is the deduplication key. Search playlist URLs and existing hub pages before creating a second page for a different name for the same playlist.
An informal list of video links without a YouTube playlist ID is a collection or series, but not a YouTube Playlist instance.

An ordered playlist declares logseq-entity:: with Logseq/Entity/YouTube/Playlist first and Logseq/Entity/Series second. The playlist hub is the one external work and the named sequence; member videos remain distinct Logseq/Entity/YouTube pages.

Prefer a hub near its member videos, often <creator>/YouTube/Series/<name>; retain a requested or established path when it is already the series hub. Put a published ordinal on members only when the playlist or publisher uses one.

Shared property conventions live on Logseq/Frontmatter. Add a verifiable date-created:: and creation-year link when the playlist's own creation date is known; the date of its oldest video does not establish the playlist's creation date.
Lead with a bullet-wrapped H1 linked to the playlist URL. Describe the scope briefly and list member video page links in playlist order when known.

logseq-created-time-year:: - links an entity to its creation year, decade, or century
The value is a link to the matching instance, at whatever precision is actually known — a specific year, or its decade or century when only that much is known.

Distinct from date-created::: that property holds the display-quality date value (day, month, or year, per ) and does not always resolve to a page. logseq-created-time-year:: always does, so every entity created in a given year, decade, or century collects there as a backlink regardless of the entity's own type.
Applies broadly, to any entity whose creation year is known: books, movies, podcast episodes, essays, musical compositions, works of art, and others.

Logseq tags have a special impact on the Logseq UI, but their implementation is buggy and inconsistent. In addition, the human gardener's use of tags:: pre-dated the more mature Logseq/Entity entity system, and the human's rules for applying them are fuzzy and ill-defined. It's easier to use them incorrectly than to use them correctly.
As a result, their use is considered protected on existing pages: AI should not modify, add, or remove it unless explicit human instruction overrides the garden tagging rules.
For new pages, add tags:: only when the relevant page-type convention explicitly requires it or nearby pages establish the same pattern.

episode pages record the MicroFreak presets created during recording. Each recorded patch keeps its saved slot, downloadable preset file and connection to the episode's audio, then receives a convention-based or creative name after recording.
Protocol evidence and current script capabilities: Microfreak/CLI/Preset metadata over USB.

Save the patch on the instrument, then record its slot on the episode page in the order the patches were created. Downloads capture the saved preset; an unsaved front-panel edit may differ from the downloaded patch.
Capture the saved name, category, slot, session order, full patch backup and sound-data fingerprint. Link an audio excerpt or a recording timestamp when available.
Keep an episode patch identifier independent of slot and device name. The same slot can later hold a different sound, and a renamed patch should retain its episode notes and audio references.
Downloading should be part of capture. Retain the original export when making later renamed exports so the episode's original sound remains recoverable.
Live validation: Microfreak/CLI/Validation/26-10-03 slot 397 records matching downloads and a parser-validated .mfpz export of Imit. MCC import and restoration remain pending.
Existing microfreak:download task downloads one populated slot through the Python/RtMidi library and saves a raw .bin backup plus a JSON manifest with metadata and checksums.
